newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-LIONS SQUAD TO REFLECT ENGLAND STRENGTH.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-LIONS SQUAD TO REFLECT ENGLAND STRENGTH.

text.p: The first British Lions squad to tour South Africa for 17 years will be dominated by Englishmen, not least several who played only minor roles in the Five Nations championship which ended on Saturday.

England's 34-13 win over Wales in their final match may not have been enough to prevent France taking the title, but their powerful victory gave the Lions selectors further proof of the talent lurking on the fringes of Jack Rowell's squad.

Bath pair Mike Catt and Jeremy Guscott, for example, started only one Five Nations game between them this year but can both be considered certainties when the 35-strong Lions squad is announced early next month.

Scrum-half Austin Healey, who made one starting appearance, and hooker Phil Greening, a second-half replacement for Mark Regan in Cardiff, will also come under strong consideration when the initial 62-man squad is trimmed by the selectors over the next fortnight.

In contrast, England captain Phil de Glanville, wings Tony Underwood and Jon Sleightholme and goalkicking fly-half Paul Grayson may all miss out, reflecting the different views of Rowell and Lions team manager Fran Cotton.

"It's totally different for him," stressed Rowell, who has steered his team to another triple crown just weeks after being accused of talking "mumbo-jumbo" by his predecessor Geoff Cooke. "We were planning for today and tomorrow. Fran Cotton has a different job to do."

There has nevertheless been widespread disbelief that Guscott, who was heavily involved in two of England's four tries in Cardiff after coming on as a second-half replacement on the wing, has not been given more opportunities.

Even Rowell, with de Glanville sitting a metre away, admitted he thought the Lions should use Guscott in the centre even though there will be strong competition from Welshmen Scott Gibbs and Allan Bateman and Scotland's Alan Tait.

The Lions, although the captaincy is still up for grabs, also look powerful in most areas of the pack and at scrum-half where Welshman Rob Howley will provide a worthy opponent for Joost van der Westhuizen.
But there remain questions to be answered at fly-half, wing and full-back, particularly after Neil Jenkins looks likely to be ruled out after breaking his arm in the match against England.

Without Jenkins, fourth in the all-time world list of pointscorers with 534 points in 50 tests, the likely test side is potentially very short on goalkickers, a further reason why the South African-born Catt could emerge as a key Lion.

His tactical kicking is distinctly mixed -- in practice before the game at Cardiff he even miscued one punt into the regimental band entertaining the crowd -- but his place-kicking is improving and he looks sharp with the ball in hand.

He certainly answered the Welsh newspaper who dismissed him as "a joke of a fly-half" on the morning of the match, and the likes of Scotland and Ireland would have loved to possess a reserve of his ability this season.

The Scots and Irish may end up sharing a mere eight Lions places, with Wales hoping for a similar allocation on their own. That would still leave England with a likely minimum of 19 representatives in a squad again coached by Scot Ian McGeechan.

Compare that with the eight Englishmen -- plus two replacements -- who toured South Africa with the Lions in 1980. Times have changed and, judging by this Five Nations season, England's old Celtic rivals are now a long way behind.
